title: When should two microservices be MERGED back (or decomposition stop) — when the boundary creates coordination without autonomy (same team, deployed together, synchronous chains, shared consistency, lockstep schema/API changes), and why should a healthy architecture be able to delete/merge services, not only create them?
shortTitle: When should two microservices be merged back

s1_definition.profdef: Two microservices should be merged back, or decomposition should stop, when the boundary between them produces coordination without autonomy. The warning signs are concrete: the same team owns both and they always change together; they are always deployed together; calls between them form synchronous request chains where one cannot function without the other being up; they share a consistency requirement that forces distributed transactions for simple operations; and schema or API changes to one force a lockstep change to the other. A healthy architecture treats merging and deleting services as first-class operations, not just creating them, because the right number of services is whatever maximizes team autonomy, and a boundary that was correct last year can become wrong as the domain evolves.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine two departments were split apart, but it turns out they share one manager, always submit their budgets together, constantly phone each other to finish a single task, must balance the same ledger, and can never change a form without the other changing the same form on the same day. They are not really two departments; they are one department pretending to be two, with couriers running pointlessly between them. The healthy move is to merge them back into one room. A good bank reorganizes departments both ways, combining them when the split added cost without benefit, not only ever splitting them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Merge two services back when the boundary causes coordination without autonomy, such as shared team, lockstep deploys, synchronous chains, shared consistency, and lockstep schema changes, and treat deleting or merging services as a normal, healthy operation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two microservices should be merged back, or decomposition should stop, when the boundary between them produces coordination without autonomy. The warning signs are concrete: the same team owns both and they always change together; they are always deployed together; calls between them form synchronous request chains where one cannot function without the other being up; they share a consistency requirement that forces distributed transactions for simple operations; and schema or API changes to one force a lockstep change to the other. A healthy architecture treats merging and deleting services as first-class operations, not just creating them, because the right number of services is whatever maximizes team autonomy, and a boundary that was correct last year can become wrong as the domain evolves.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine two departments were split apart, but it turns out they share one manager, always submit their budgets together, constantly phone each other to finish a single task, must balance the same ledger, and can never change a form without the other changing the same form on the same day. They are not really two departments; they are one department pretending to be two, with couriers running pointlessly between them. The healthy move is to merge them back into one room. A good bank reorganizes departments both ways, combining them when the split added cost without benefit, not only ever splitting them.

**One line to remember:** Merge two services back when the boundary causes coordination without autonomy, such as shared team, lockstep deploys, synchronous chains, shared consistency, and lockstep schema changes, and treat deleting or merging services as a normal, healthy operation.

sections.s2_technical:
The first signal is a shared team and shared change cadence. If one team owns both services and nearly every feature touches both, the split is not buying independent deployment, it is just adding network hops and coordination. Microservices exist to let teams move independently, so if the people and the changes are shared, the boundary is fighting the organization.

The second signal is lockstep deployment. If you can never deploy service A without deploying service B at the same time, you do not have two independently deployable services, you have a distributed monolith. You verify this by asking whether a release of one has ever gone to production alone. If the honest answer is never, the boundary is fake.

The third signal is synchronous request chains. If every call to service A immediately makes a blocking call to service B, and A is useless when B is down, then A and B are effectively one unit of availability. Splitting them did not improve resilience; it made it worse, because now there are two processes and a network link that can all fail, instead of one in-process call that cannot. The fourth signal is shared consistency: if a single simple operation must update data in both services atomically, you are forced into a saga or a two-phase dance for something that should be one local transaction, paying huge complexity for an invariant that wants to live in one place.

The fifth signal is lockstep schema or API changes: if changing a column or a contract in one service always forces a coordinated change in the other, the model was never truly separated. When several of these signals appear together, the fix is to merge the services: combine the codebases, merge the databases if they were artificially split, and replace the network calls with in-process method calls, which also removes the serialization, latency, and partial-failure cost. The senior-level nuance, and the part interviewers love, is that a healthy architecture must be able to delete and merge services, not only create them. The correct number of services is not maximal; it is whatever maximizes autonomy for the current team structure and domain. Boundaries are hypotheses, and a mature team revises a wrong hypothesis by merging back without ego.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a `LimitCheck` service and a `Transfer` service were split, but problems appeared. Problem 1 — every single transfer makes a synchronous blocking call to the limit-check service, and if limit-check is down, no transfer can proceed, so they share one availability fate. This is exactly the synchronous-chain signal. Problem 2 — the same two-person team owns both and every feature changes both, always deployed together. This is exactly the shared-team and lockstep-deploy signal. Problem 3 — a new limit rule requires a schema change in both services at once. This is exactly the lockstep-schema signal. Together these say: merge them.

The mini-project models a `BoundaryHealthAnalyzer` that scores a boundary against the five signals and recommends merge or keep, a `SplitTransferService` and `LimitCheckService` showing the costly synchronous chain, and a `MergedTransferService` showing the same logic as one in-process call. A runnable demo scores the boundary, demonstrates the fragile split when limit-check is down, and shows the merged service working as one unit.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a boundary with all five signals present, then a 50,000 transfer from Rajesh in both the split and the merged designs.

Step 1: The analyzer evaluates the boundary against the five signals: same team, deployed together, synchronous chain, shared consistency, and lockstep schema. All five are present, so it scores five out of five and recommends MERGE.

Step 2: In the split design, a healthy transfer makes a blocking remote call to the limit-check service, which approves it, and the transfer completes. The network hop works, but it was pure overhead because the check could have been local.

Step 3: The limit-check service goes down. The split transfer makes its blocking call, the call throws, and the transfer is blocked entirely. The two services share one availability fate, so splitting made resilience worse, not better.

Step 4: In the merged design, the same transfer runs the limit check as an in-process method call inside one local transaction. There is no network hop, no circuit breaker, and no shared-fate dependency.

Step 5: The merged transfer completes. The business logic is identical, but it is now simpler, faster, and more resilient, which is exactly why merging back was the right call when the boundary produced coordination without autonomy.

```text

Oct 24, 2026 11:53:40 WARNING MERGE: 5/5 signals — coordination without autonomy
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:40 INFO Recommendation: MERGE

Oct 24, 2026 11:53:40 INFO SPLIT transfer 50000 from SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:40 INFO Healthy: COMPLETED
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I tell interviewers that knowing when to merge services back is just as important as knowing when to split them, and most engineers only ever learn the splitting half. Two microservices should be merged back when the boundary between them produces coordination without autonomy, and there are five concrete signals I look for. The first is a shared team and shared change cadence: if one team owns both and nearly every feature touches both, the split is not buying independent deployment, it is just adding coordination. The second is lockstep deployment: if I can never release one without releasing the other at the same time, I have a distributed monolith, not two services.

The third signal is a synchronous request chain. At National Bank of India we once split a limit-check service out of the transfer service, and every single transfer made a blocking call to it, so when limit-check was down no transfer could proceed. The two services shared one availability fate, which means the split actually made resilience worse, because now there were two processes and a network link that could all fail instead of one in-process call that could not. The fourth signal is shared consistency, where a single simple operation must update both services atomically, forcing a saga for something that wanted to be one local transaction. The fifth is lockstep schema or API changes, where changing a column in one always forces a coordinated change in the other.

When several of these signals appear together, I merge the services: I combine the codebases, merge the databases that were artificially split, and replace the network calls with in-process method calls, which removes the latency, serialization, and partial-failure cost all at once. In the limit-check example, merging turned a fragile distributed check into one resilient local transaction with identical business logic.

The deeper principle I always emphasize is that a healthy architecture must be able to delete and merge services, not only create them. The correct number of services is not the maximum; it is whatever maximizes autonomy for the current team structure and domain. Boundaries are hypotheses, and a boundary that was right last year can be wrong this year as the domain evolves. A mature team revises a wrong hypothesis by merging back without ego, rather than defending a split that is quietly taxing every request.
